facts.statement: Wamweracaudia lived 155 to 145 million years ago in the Late Jurassic of Tanzania, Africa.
facts.quote: Wamweracaudia is a large herbivorous sauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic (155-145 million years ago) Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania, Africa.

facts.statement: A sauropod tail was excavated at Site G during German expeditions to Tendaguru between 1909 and 1912 under the supervision of Werner Janensch.
facts.quote: During the German expeditions to the Tendaguru in German East Africa between 1909 and 1912, paleontologist Werner Janensch supervised the excavation of a sauropod tail at "Site G".

facts.statement: Werner Janensch referred the tail to Gigantosaurus robustus in 1929.
facts.quote: In 1929, he referred this tail to Gigantosaurus robustus.

facts.statement: The tail was assigned to the separate genus Janenschia in 1991.
facts.quote: In 1991, G. robustus was made the separate genus Janenschia.

facts.statement: The specimen was named Wamweracaudia keranjei in 2019 by Mannion, Upchurch, Schwarz, and Wings.
facts.quote: The specimen was in 2019 given the new genus and species name Wamweracaudia keranjei by Philip D. Mannion, Paul Upchurch, Daniela Schwarz and Oliver Wings in their re-appraisal of Janenschia and other presumed titanosaur finds from the Tendaguru.

facts.statement: The genus name Wamweracaudia combines the name of the Wamwera tribe with the Latin word for tail.
facts.quote: The generic name combines a reference to the Wamwera, a tribe inhabiting the region of the find, with a Latin cauda, "tail".

facts.statement: The species name keranjei honors Mohammadi Keranje, the foreman who led the excavation team.
facts.quote: The specific name honours the native foreman leading the team that excavated the tail, Mohammadi Keranje.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of specimens MB.R.2091.1–30, MB.R.3817.1, and MB.R.3817.2 found in the Tithonian layer of the Tendaguru Formation.
facts.quote: Wamweracaudia is known from the holotype MB.R.2091.1–30, MB.R.3817.1 & MB.R.3817.2, found in a layer of the Tendagaru Formation dating from the Tithonian.

facts.statement: Researchers believe one vertebra is missing from the known series of tail bones.
facts.quote: Probably one vertebra is missing from the series.

facts.statement: The authors identified four unique derived traits (autapomorphies) for Wamweracaudia.
facts.quote: The describing authors established four autapomorphies, unique derived traits.

facts.statement: The upper surface of the front and middle tail vertebrae is excavated at the rear.
facts.quote: With the front and middle tail vertebrae, the upper surface is excavated at its rear.

facts.statement: The neural processes of the front tail vertebrae have a rough zone on the upper third of the side surface separated from the rear rough zone by a vertical groove.
facts.quote: With the front tail vertebrae, the neural processes show a rough zone on the upper third part of their side surface, separated from the rough zone of the rear surface by a vertical groove.

facts.statement: The underside of the middle to rear vertebrae is strongly pinched transversely, forming a ridge rather than a flat surface.
facts.quote: With the middle to rear vertebrae, the underside is strongly pinched transversely, forming a ridge instead of a distinct flat surface.

facts.statement: A pair of small extensions called tubercula is present on the top rib facet of the front tail vertebrae between the prezygapophysis and diapophysis.
facts.quote: With the front tail vertebrae, just in between the outer side of the prezygapophysis and the tip of the upper side of the diapophysis, the top rib facet, a pair of small extensions, or tubercula, is present.

facts.statement: Cladistic analysis places Wamweracaudia in the family Mamenchisauridae as a sister species of Mamenchisaurus.
facts.quote: An exact cladistic analysis, part of the 2019 study, showed that Wamweracaudia was placed in the Mamenchisauridae, as a sister species of Mamenchisaurus.

facts.statement: Wamweracaudia and Mamenchisaurus share procoelous tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The two taxa shared procoelous tail vertebrae.

facts.statement: As a sauropod, Wamweracaudia was a large quadrupedal herbivore.
facts.quote: As a sauropod, Wamweracaudia would have been a large quadrupedal herbivore.

facts.statement: It is debated whether two additional traits are autapomorphies, pending confirmation that Wamweracaudia is a mamenchisaurid.
facts.quote: Two additional traits are autapomorphies if Wamweracaudia is indeed a mamenchisaurid.

facts.statement: The genus Wamweracaudia was named by Mannion and colleagues in 2019.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Wamweracaudia (genus), Mannion et al. 2019

facts.statement: Wamweracaudia belongs to the family Mamenchisauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Mamenchisauridae

facts.statement: Wamweracaudia is classified within the dinosaur class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: Wamweracaudia lived during the Tithonian stage, between 149.2 and 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Tithonian to Tithonian (149.2 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are two recorded fossil occurrences of Wamweracaudia.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 2

facts.statement: Research by Beeston et al. in 2026 indicates that Wamweracaudia keranjei exhibits pneumaticity in its anterior caudal vertebrae, a trait showing at least five independent origins or reversals in Neosauropoda.
facts.quote: A study on the caudal vertebrae of Cetiosaurus sp., "Cetiosaurus" glymptonensis, Wamweracaudia keranjei, Dicraeosaurus sattleri, Tornieria africana and Giraffatitan brancai, providing evidence of at least five independent origins and/or reversals of pneumaticity of anterior caudal vertebrae in Neosauropoda, is published by Beeston et al. (2026).
